answer_text:
Assume “independent” means mutually independent.

Let the events be \(A_1,\dots,A_n\), with

\[
0<P(A_i)<1 \qquad (i=1,\dots,n).
\]

For each choice of signs

\[
\varepsilon=(\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_n)\in\{0,1\}^n,
\]

define the atom

\[
B_\varepsilon
=
\bigcap_{i:\varepsilon_i=1} A_i
\;\cap\;
\bigcap_{i:\varepsilon_i=0} A_i^c.
\]

These \(2^n\) sets are pairwise disjoint. Because replacing independent events by their complements preserves independence, the \(2^n\) choices are all independent in the sense that

\[
P(B_\varepsilon)
=
\prod_{i=1}^n
\begin{cases}
P(A_i), & \varepsilon_i=1,\\
P(A_i^c), & \varepsilon_i=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Since \(0<P(A_i)<1\), every factor is positive, so

\[
P(B_\varepsilon)>0
\]

for every \(\varepsilon\in\{0,1\}^n\).

Thus the sample space must contain at least one distinct point in each of these \(2^n\) disjoint positive-probability sets. Therefore any such sample space must have at least

\[
2^n
\]

points.

This bound is attainable: take

\[
\Omega=\{0,1\}^n
\]

with uniform probability, and let

\[
A_i=\{\omega\in\Omega:\omega_i=1\}.
\]

Then each \(A_i\) has probability \(1/2\), and the events are independent.

Hence the minimum number of points is

\[
\boxed{2^n}.
\]
